hero.subtitle: The universal syntax for identifying resources on the Internet

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) provides a simple and extensible means for identifying a resource. This specification defines the generic URI syntax and the process for resolving URI references.

URIs are the foundation of the Web. Every URL you type in a browser, every API endpoint, and every resource link follows this specification. Understanding URI syntax is essential for web development and Internet protocols.

sections.title: Characters
sections.content:
URIs are composed of a limited set of characters. Characters outside this set must be percent-encoded.

UnreservedA-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~
Reserved (gen-delims): / ? # [ ] @
Reserved (sub-delims)! $ & ' ( ) * + , ; =
Percent-Encoding Examples
Space       -> %20
Forward /   -> %2F (in path segments)
Question ?  -> %3F (in path)
Ampersand & -> %26 (in query values)
UTF-8 char  -> %E2%9C%93 (checkmark)

sections.title: Syntax Components
sections.content:
The generic URI syntax consists of a hierarchical sequence of five components:

URI Component Breakdown
         foo://example.com:8042/over/there?name=ferret#nose
         \_/   \______________/\_________/ \_________/ \__/
          |           |            |            |        |
       scheme     authority       path        query   fragment
schemeIdentifies the protocol (http, https, ftp, mailto, etc.)Required
authority[userinfo@]host[:port] - identifies the serverOptional
pathHierarchical path to the resourceRequired (may be empty)
queryNon-hierarchical key-value parametersOptional
fragmentSecondary resource identifier (client-side only)Optional

sections.title: Reference Resolution
sections.content:
Relative references allow URIs to be expressed relative to a base URI. The resolution algorithm transforms a relative reference into its target URI.

Reference Resolution Examples
Base URI: http://a/b/c/d;p?q

"g:h"       -> g:h            (different scheme)
"g"         -> http://a/b/c/g  (relative path)
"./g"       -> http://a/b/c/g  (same as above)
"../g"      -> http://a/b/g    (parent directory)
"//g"       -> http://g        (network-path)
"?y"        -> http://a/b/c/d;p?y  (query override)
"#s"        -> http://a/b/c/d;p?q#s (fragment only)

Relative references are heavily used in HTML (links, images, stylesheets) and HTTP (Location header redirects). The resolution algorithm must handle edge cases like empty paths, double dots, and scheme-relative references.

sections.title: Normalization
sections.content:
URI normalization converts URIs into a canonical form, enabling comparison of URIs that may be syntactically different but semantically equivalent.

Case Normalization
Scheme and host are case-insensitive and should be lowercased. Percent-encoding hex digits should be uppercased (e.g., %2f -> %2F).
Percent-Encoding Normalization
Unreserved characters that are percent-encoded should be decoded (e.g., %41 -> A).
Path Segment Normalization
Dot segments (. and ..) in the path should be resolved and removed.
Port Normalization
Default ports should be removed (e.g., http://example.com:80/ -> http://example.com/).

sections.title: URI, URL, and URN
sections.content:
The terms URI, URL, and URN are often confused. This specification clarifies their relationship.

Term
Description
Example
URI
Generic identifier for any resource
Any URL or URN
URL
URI that provides location/access mechanism
https://example.com/page
URN
URI that provides persistent name
urn:isbn:0451450523

In practice, the terms URI and URL are often used interchangeably. The distinction matters primarily in formal specifications. All URLs are URIs, and all URNs are URIs, but not all URIs are URLs or URNs.

references.text: Berners-Lee, T., "Universal Resource Identifiers in WWW", RFC 1630, June 1994.
Fielding, R., "Relative Uniform Resource Locators", RFC 1808, June 1995.
